planner.clinicalAnchor: A patient with a symptomatic unilateral effusion is being prepared for ultrasound-guided thoracentesis. The team must choose a safe window, review bleeding risk, and decide when drainage should slow or stop.
planner.keyTakeaway: Ultrasound confirms where to enter; ongoing symptoms and pressure behavior decide how drainage proceeds. Bleeding decisions still require indication, urgency, medication timing, and local policy.
planner.stopSlow: Stop or slow drainage when symptoms, very negative pressure, or rapid large-volume removal raises concern.
planner.triangleBody: Use the diagram to rehearse the lateral window bounded by pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi, the axilla, rib spaces, and the diaphragm.

gradual.label: Gradual pressure decline
gradual.description: Drainage is tolerated until higher volumes or symptoms appear.

biphasic.label: Late steep pressure drop
biphasic.description: Early drainage looks reasonable, then pressure falls faster.

earlyNegativePressure.label: Early negative-pressure warning
earlyNegativePressure.description: Symptoms and marked pressure drop can appear with small volumes.

triangle.title: Triangle of safety diagram
triangle.desc: Educational chest wall diagram showing pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi, axilla, diaphragm boundary, rib spaces, and a preferred lateral ultrasound window.

posterior-medial.label: Posterior/medial
posterior-medial.teachingPoint: Posterior and medial approaches near the spine have more variable, exposed intercostal vessels; scan laterally for a safer window.

too-low.label: Below safe diaphragm boundary
too-low.teachingPoint: A low entry risks diaphragm and abdominal structures; re-map the pocket and keep the diaphragm visible.

mid-axillary.label: Mid-axillary
mid-axillary.teachingPoint: Mid-axillary access can be appropriate when ultrasound confirms fluid depth, rib-space anatomy, and diaphragm location.

lateral-safe.label: Lateral ultrasound-confirmed window
lateral-safe.teachingPoint: A lateral ultrasound-confirmed pocket with a clear diaphragm boundary is the preferred teaching target.

drainageTeaching.expandable: Expandable lung shows a gradual pressure decline and symptom-limited drainage.
drainageTeaching.partiallyExpandable: Partially expandable lung has a biphasic curve: early drainage looks tolerable, then pressure falls faster.
drainageTeaching.trapped: Trapped lung starts negative and becomes steeply negative with small drainage volumes; symptoms can occur early.

pathway.predictHeading: Predict the disposition before revealing the comparison
pathway.keyTakeaway: ACCP 2001 is useful as a historical size-and-stability comparator. BTS 2023 places more emphasis on symptoms, patient priorities, ambulatory pathways, and reliable follow-up.

headline.escalatePal: Specialist escalation for persistent air leak
headline.shortTermDrainage: Short-term drainage for rapid symptom relief

rationale.accpStabilityNotMet: American College of Chest Physicians stability criteria are not met, so physiology takes priority over size.
rationale.accpPalEarly: The 2001 framework escalates persistent air leak earlier, around days 3 to 5 after drainage and system checks.
rationale.accpSspReserve: Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax has less respiratory reserve, so the historical framework favors drainage and monitoring.
rationale.accpStableVitals: The patient meets the historical stable-patient vital sign criteria.
rationale.accpSmallPspObserve: Small primary spontaneous pneumothorax is observation territory in ACCP 2001.
rationale.accpLargeOrSymptomatic: Large size or meaningful symptoms move the historical pathway toward aspiration or drainage.
rationale.btsTensionEmergency: British Thoracic Society guidance treats tension physiology or significant hypoxia as a high-risk emergency.
rationale.btsPalWindow: The 2023 pathway uses time-bounded reassessment and escalation when an air leak persists around days 5 to 7.
rationale.btsHighRiskContext: High-risk characteristics, including underlying lung disease or ventilated/traumatic context, favor monitored intervention.
rationale.btsSizeDeemphasized: The 2023 pathway de-emphasizes size for stable, minimally symptomatic primary spontaneous pneumothorax.
rationale.btsProcedureAvoidance: Procedure avoidance is reasonable when follow-up and return precautions are reliable.
rationale.btsSevereRelief: Severe symptoms shift the patient-priority question toward rapid relief and monitored drainage.
rationale.btsStableSymptomaticChoice: For stable symptomatic primary spontaneous pneumothorax, the pathway weighs patient preference, local availability, and rapid symptom relief.

comparisonNote.converge: Both frameworks converge here, which usually means physiology, high-risk context, or persistent air leak timing is dominating the decision.
comparisonNote.sizeVsSymptom: Classic divergence: ACCP 2001 reacts to size, while BTS 2023 prioritizes symptoms, patient priorities, and follow-up reliability.
comparisonNote.palTiming: The divergence is timing: ACCP 2001 escalates persistent air leak before the BTS 2023 day-5 window.
comparisonNote.genericDivergence: The frameworks diverge; identify whether size, symptom burden, local ambulatory care, or risk context is driving the difference.

recurrencePrevention.highRiskOccupation: High-risk occupation, such as aviation or diving, lowers the threshold for definitive recurrence-prevention discussion.
recurrencePrevention.recurrenceOrSsp: Recurrence or secondary spontaneous pneumothorax should prompt prevention counseling, smoking cessation, pleurodesis or surgical options, and specialist follow-up.
recurrencePrevention.firstPsp: For a first primary spontaneous pneumothorax, counsel about recurrence risk, smoking cessation, follow-up, and return precautions.

differential.title: Adjust the diagnostic lens
differential.lensHelp: Lower context settings show a broader pattern match. Higher settings reward the bedside story and ultrasound, so the list narrows around the current clinical frame.

quiz.title: Match the pleural findings to the disease
quiz.emptyState: Choose the diagnosis most associated with the full pattern. The rare items are mixed in on purpose; the goal is not memorizing a single lab cutoff, it is recognizing when a clue changes the branch.

headlineCode.pseudoexudate: Light's criteria are positive, but reconciliation favors a pseudoexudate.
headlineCode.definitiveSignal: {diagnosis} has a specific pleural fluid signal.
headlineCode.exudatePattern: This is an exudative pattern; now narrow it with clinical context.
headlineCode.transudatePattern: This is a transudative pattern unless the clinical story says otherwise.

reconciliationCode.tooSmall: A very small effusion is usually a sampling decision before it is a chemistry decision.
reconciliationCode.pseudoexudate: The chemistry label diverges from the bedside story. In this setting, gradients and NT-proBNP help avoid unnecessary invasive workup for a diuresed systemic effusion.
reconciliationCode.transudateButPretest: The chemistry looks transudative, but the clinical pretest probability is not low. Malignancy and other competing processes can occasionally look deceptively bland.
reconciliationCode.exudateInfection: The exudate label is expected, but pH, glucose, LDH, ultrasound, and cultures determine whether this behaves like pleural infection needing drainage.
reconciliationCode.exudateTb: The exudate label is only the first fork. Lymphocyte predominance, exposure history, ADA, and pleural biopsy strategy carry the diagnosis forward.
reconciliationCode.transudateAligned: The chemistry and initial frame align with altered systemic pressure or oncotic forces; still check for unilateral, bloody, nodular, or recurrent features that break the pattern.
reconciliationCode.probabilityShifter: PFA should be interpreted as a probability shifter: it narrows the search, then history, imaging, and selected tests finish the reasoning.

pseudoexudateReason.weaklyPositive: Light criteria are only weakly positive in a systemic transudate context

empyema.rationale: Gross pus in pleural fluid is diagnostic of pleural space infection.
empyema.action: Drain the pleural space and treat as pleural infection; send microbiology if not already done.

malignantEffusion.rationale: Positive pleural fluid cytology establishes pleural malignancy in the right clinical setting.
malignantEffusion.action: Stage the malignancy, match management to prognosis and symptoms, and consider molecular testing when appropriate.

chylothorax.rationale: Pleural triglycerides above 110 mg/dL, or intermediate triglycerides with chylomicrons, support chyle in the pleural space.
chylothorax.action: Look for trauma, thoracic surgery, lymphoma, lymphatic disorders, or cirrhosis-related transudative chylothorax.

hemothorax.rationale: Pleural fluid hematocrit more than 50% of blood hematocrit defines hemothorax.
hemothorax.action: Escalate source control and drainage planning; evaluate trauma, procedure injury, malignancy, or anticoagulation.

urinothoraxCreatinine.rationale: Pleural-to-serum creatinine ratio above 1 supports urine tracking into the pleural space.
urinothoraxCreatinine.action: Evaluate obstructive uropathy or genitourinary injury; pleural drainage alone usually recurs.

bilothorax.rationale: Pleural-to-serum bilirubin ratio above 1 supports bile in the pleural space.
bilothorax.action: Search for biliary pathology or recent hepatobiliary surgery and coordinate definitive source control.

pancreaticopleuralFistula.rationale: Very high pleural amylase strongly suggests pancreatic fluid entering the pleural space.
pancreaticopleuralFistula.action: Evaluate chronic pancreatitis, pseudocyst, and duct leak; abdominal imaging and pancreatic consultation usually matter more than repeat taps.

esophagealPerforation.rationale: Food particles in pleural fluid are a high-specificity clue for esophageal rupture.
esophagealPerforation.action: Escalate urgently for source control, broad antimicrobials, and esophageal evaluation.

urinothoraxOdor.rationale: A urine odor is a classic gross inspection clue, especially with ipsilateral urinary tract obstruction or injury.
urinothoraxOdor.action: Check pleural-to-serum creatinine and evaluate the urinary tract.

parapneumonic.rationale: Pneumonia context plus low pH, low glucose, high LDH, high nucleated cells, or positive microbiology points toward pleural infection.
parapneumonic.action: Do not let Light criteria be the endpoint; assess need for tube drainage, culture-directed antibiotics, and loculation management.

tuberculous.rationale: A lymphocyte-predominant exudate with compatible exposure history and elevated ADA narrows the differential toward TB.
tuberculous.action: Send mycobacterial culture when suspected; if suspicion remains high, pleural biopsy can secure microbiology and drug susceptibility.

malignancyInPlay.rationale: Pleural nodularity or a strong cancer context can outweigh a nonspecific or even transudative chemistry profile.
malignancyInPlay.action: Send adequate cytology volume and consider image-guided or thoracoscopic pleural biopsy if cytology is negative and pretest probability stays high.

repeatedNegativeCytology.rationale: Two nondiagnostic cytology samples do not rule out malignant pleural disease when imaging or clinical probability remains high.
repeatedNegativeCytology.action: Stop fluid-only cycling and escalate toward pleural tissue diagnosis such as image-guided biopsy or pleuroscopy.

autoimmunePleuritis.rationale: Autoimmune context with low pH, low glucose, or high LDH can mimic pleural infection.
autoimmunePleuritis.action: Reconcile with serologies, joint/systemic activity, microbiology, and imaging before anchoring on infection alone.

eosinophilic.rationale: Pleural eosinophils above 10% suggest air or blood in the pleural space, prior thoracentesis, drug reaction, asbestos exposure, parasites, infection, or malignancy.
eosinophilic.action: Use the history and gross appearance to decide whether this is procedure-related noise or a diagnostic clue.

lymphocytePredominant.rationale: Marked lymphocyte predominance narrows the differential to TB, lymphoma, sarcoidosis, chylothorax, trapped lung, post-CABG, yellow nail syndrome, uremia, drug causes, and rheumatoid disease.
lymphocytePredominant.action: Let timeline, exposure, imaging, and targeted tests decide the next fork.

lymphaticLeak.rationale: Milky or turbid pleural fluid with a surgery, lymphoma, lymphatic, or yellow-nail context should trigger lipid testing.
lymphaticLeak.action: Check triglycerides, cholesterol, and chylomicrons rather than relying on appearance alone.

bloodInPleuralSpace.rationale: Bloody fluid can be caused by malignancy, pulmonary embolism, trauma, post-cardiotomy injury, asbestos pleuritis, or hemothorax.
bloodInPleuralSpace.action: Measure pleural hematocrit when grossly bloody; do not treat all serosanguineous fluid as hemothorax.

tooSmall: Confirm whether the effusion is safely sampleable with ultrasound.
Treat or observe the likely cause if the effusion is < 1 cm and the patient is clinically stable.
bilateralSystemic: Treat the systemic cause when the story is obvious and the effusions are bilateral and anechoic.
Sample if the course, laterality, fever, pleuritic pain, or imaging no longer fits the systemic diagnosis.
nextActions.definitiveFollowUp: Use the remaining PFA data to identify concurrent processes and management risk.
pseudoexudate: Reclassify cautiously as likely systemic transudate and treat the underlying CHF, renal, hepatic, or oncotic driver.
Reassess response; sample or image further if the effusion persists, is unilateral, becomes bloody, or develops pleural thickening.
infection: Use pleural pH, glucose, LDH, culture yield, and ultrasound loculation to decide drainage urgency.
Inoculate pleural fluid into blood culture bottles when pleural infection is suspected.
tb: Send AFB smear and culture, but plan around low culture yield and delayed results.
If suspicion stays high, pursue pleural biopsy for histology, culture, and drug susceptibility.
malignancyEscalate: Stop fluid-only cycling and move toward pleural tissue diagnosis with image-guided biopsy or pleuroscopy.
Use lung expansion, symptoms, prognosis, and patient goals to choose IPC, pleurodesis, or combined strategy.
malignancyCytology: Send adequate cytology volume and review CT or ultrasound for pleural targets.
If cytology is negative but pleural nodularity or cancer history remains convincing, move toward pleural biopsy.
transudate: Focus on CHF, renal, hepatic, oncotic, peritoneal, and trapped-lung physiology.
Avoid repeated diagnostic taps unless the clinical course stops fitting a transudate.
exudateGeneric: Use the exudate label to choose a targeted branch: infection, malignancy, TB, pulmonary embolism, autoimmune disease, post-procedure, or abdominal source.
Repeat thoracentesis, observe, treat empirically, or biopsy based on the remaining probability after clinical reconciliation.

pitfalls.pairedSerum: Do not interpret pleural chemistry without the paired serum values and the pre-thoracentesis clinical impression.
pitfalls.diuresisCrossesLight: Diuresis and systemic effusions can cross Light criteria by a small margin.
pitfalls.systemicGradientCheck: A systemic transudate context with positive Light criteria should trigger a gradient check before anchoring on an exudate.
pitfalls.fragilePH: Pleural pH is fragile; delayed analysis, air, or lidocaine contamination can change the result.
pitfalls.milkyTurbid: Milky or turbid fluid can be chyle, cholesterol, empyema, or cellular debris.
pitfalls.negativeCytology: Negative cytology does not rule out malignant pleural disease when imaging or history is convincing.
pitfalls.repeatedCytologyDelay: After two nondiagnostic cytology samples, repeated fluid-only testing can delay needed pleural tissue diagnosis.

assembly.accessoryInstrumentRouteDescription: BPS semi-rigid forceps and other compatible slender accessories may enter through a BB2401/BB2402 gate; this route is distinct from both ventilation ports.

assembly.assemblyModeDescription: Choose from every loose piece and connect it to the correct interface.

assembly.egressBlockedDescription: A fixed complete occlusion blocks distal inspiratory entry as well as expiratory return; use the separate ball-valve state to model inspiratory passage with restricted expiration.
assembly.egressOpenDescription: Expiratory gas returns from the lungs through the unobstructed distal airway and tube, then exits through the configured proximal outlet.
assembly.instrumentRouteDescription: Choose the required configuration, then trace the real instrument through either the main axial route or the smaller accessory gate. Neither ventilation port is an instrument route.
assembly.jetVentilationPortDescription: Dedicated inlet for jet pulses; it is not an instrument route.
assembly.mainAxialPortDescription: Large-bore horizontal route for the telescope plus compatible optical forceps, suction, or another configuration-specific instrument through the selected main cap.
assembly.obstructionBallValveDescription: Inspiration passes the dynamic narrowing, but expiration is restricted; retained distal gas increases across modeled breaths.
assembly.obstructionFixedCompleteDescription: The fixed occlusion blocks distal inspiratory entry and expiratory return.
assembly.obstructionOpenDescription: Inspiration reaches the distal airway and expiration can leave without modeled restriction.
assembly.opticsLightDescription: Follow illumination from the light cable to the distal field and the returning image through the telescope to the camera head.
assembly.pairedTracheoscopePatternDescription: Matched BT2205-3 tracheal tube, 260 mm, 8.0/7.0 mm, for direct diameter comparison with BT2105-3; it has no distal side fenestrations.
assembly.pathSafetyNote: Schematic pathways only—not a gas-flow, pressure, caliber, or compatibility simulator. Actual ventilation and accessory use depend on anatomy, obstruction, the exact device setup, manufacturer instructions, procedural conditions, and clinical judgment.
assembly.pathwayHelp: Play each route, pause at any point, or switch on the cutaway to see the pathway inside the assembled bronchoscope.
assembly.pathwayModeDescription: Animate ventilation, instrument travel, and the optical-light path through the assembled set.
assembly.portLayoutVariationNote: Port locations and cap systems vary by manufacturer. These labels apply to the EFER universal barrel shown.

assembly.proceduralPoseDisclaimer: Procedural poses are discrete teaching views, not a continuous insertion path. The rigid tube remains straight; do not infer that it bends or passes through the carina.
assembly.safetyNote: Educational reconstruction only. Confirm the current manufacturer instructions for use, compatibility, and local equipment checks before clinical use.
assembly.title: Assemble a rigid bronchoscopy set
assembly.toolModeDescription: Compare the shape, scale, and function of commonly used rigid instruments.
assembly.viewHelp: Drag empty space using Orbit or Pan. Scroll or pinch to zoom toward the pointer.
assembly.ventilationFlowDescription: Compare four clinically coherent respiratory cycles, true-scale tube geometry, validated procedural poses, proximal leak, and three distal-obstruction states.
assembly.bronchoscopePatternDescription: Matched BT2105-3 bronchial tube, 360 mm, 8.0/7.0 mm, for the validated mainstem demonstration.
assembly.controlledProximalLeak: Controlled breaths enter and return through the large anesthesia-circuit port with the selected proximal caps sealed. The uncuffed tube can still leak around the larynx or an incompletely sealed proximal interface; residual leak is not quantified.
assembly.conventionalVentilationDescription: Intermittent positive-pressure inspiration and expiration use the large anesthesia-circuit port with the proximal instrument openings appropriately sealed.
assembly.highFrequencyJetVentilationDescription: Rapid small-volume jets form a high-frequency pulse pattern; expiration remains passive.
assembly.leakEgressContrast: Do not confuse proximal leak with blocked expiratory egress: leak can reduce delivery; blocked egress can trap gas.
assembly.lowFrequencyJetVentilationDescription: Discrete high-velocity jets are delivered at lower frequency; expiration remains passive.
assembly.majorFenestrationLeak: In this shallow position, distal fenestrations lie above the cords and add an escape route. This may increase leak and reduce distal delivery; the magnitude is not calculated.
assembly.positionAtCarinaDescription: The distal tip sits at the tracheal bifurcation.
assembly.positionMidTracheaDescription: The BT2203 tracheoscope bevel is centered in the purpose-built tracheal lumen.
assembly.positionPastCarinaDescription: A validated bronchial-tube pose places the straight distal tube in the selected main bronchus without interpolating it through the carina.
assembly.positionRightMainstemDescription: The BT2105 bronchial tube is shown in its discrete validated right-mainstem pose.
assembly.positionLeftMainstemDescription: The BT2105 bronchial tube is shown in its discrete validated left-mainstem pose.
assembly.positionProximalTracheaDescription: The tube is seated through the cords in a shallow proximal position.
assembly.predictBothBranches: Both main bronchi remain downstream of the tube tip
assembly.predictContralateralFenestrations: The opposite main bronchus remains reachable through bronchoscope fenestrations
assembly.predictMainstemOnly: Only the entered main bronchus has a direct distal route
assembly.predictionPrompt: Before considering the separate egress warning, which anatomical distal branch route do the tube and tip position provide?
assembly.predictionReconsider: Compare your prediction with the highlighted route.
assembly.predictionResetNotice: Scenario changed. Make a new prediction before revealing flow.
assembly.resultBothBranches: Anatomically, both main bronchi remain downstream of the tube tip, so two distal branch routes are available before egress is considered.
assembly.resultContralateralFenestrations: Anatomically, the distal lumen serves the entered main bronchus while fenestrations at the correct depth and rotation preserve a route toward the opposite main bronchus.
assembly.resultMainstemOnly: Anatomically, the tracheoscope has no distal fenestration route, so after mainstem entry only the entered main bronchus has a direct distal route. Its uncuffed proximal seal may still leak.
assembly.sidePortAvailable: Bronchial-tube fenestrations at the correct depth and rotation preserve a modeled route toward the opposite main bronchus.
assembly.sidePortNotApplicable: The tip has not entered a main bronchus, so contralateral fenestrations are not the deciding feature.
assembly.sidePortUnavailable: This tracheoscope has no distal fenestration route toward the opposite main bronchus after mainstem entry.
assembly.spontaneousAssistVentilationDescription: Patient-generated inspiration continues through the breathing circuit, with separate manual or pressure-assist events delivered through the same anesthesia-circuit port—not the main axial instrument port.
assembly.openSystemProximalLeak: Some spontaneous-assisted and jet configurations retain an open proximal outlet, but their inlets remain distinct: assistance uses the anesthesia circuit and jet pulses use the fixed jet port. Delivery is not quantified.
assembly.tracheoscopePatternDescription: Matched BT2203-3 tracheal tube, 260 mm, 10.0/9.2 mm.
assembly.tracheoscopeMainstemCaution: Counterfactual comparison (geometry matched): advancing this short tracheal tube into a main bronchus is not its intended use or a validated clinical configuration.

alteplaseOnly.effect: Single-agent fibrinolytic therapy did not show the same MIST2 teaching benefit.
alteplaseOnly.caution: Avoid teaching monotherapy as the preferred pathway.

dnaseOnly.label: DNase alone
dnaseOnly.effect: DNase monotherapy is a teaching trap and was not beneficial in MIST2.
dnaseOnly.caution: Use combination therapy or an alternative strategy rather than DNase alone.

salineIrrigation.label: Pleural irrigation
salineIrrigation.effect: Normal saline irrigation is a pilot-data alternative to discuss when lytics are unsuitable or bleeding risk cannot be mitigated.
salineIrrigation.caution: Frame as selected-pathway teaching, not universal replacement for lytics or surgery.

placebo.label: Placebo / drainage alone
placebo.effect: Drainage alone can be sufficient when source control is achieved, but residual collections need early reassessment.
placebo.caution: Do not delay escalation when fever, inflammatory markers, output, or imaging fail to improve.

bleedingNote.anticoagulated: Therapeutic anticoagulation increases bleeding concern and should trigger mitigation planning.

pathway.reflectionBody: Every endpoint should ask what matters more for this patient: hospital-free days, device-free chest, speed of relief, home support, expected prognosis, infection burden, and willingness to manage a catheter.

twoPlus.recommendation: Stop fluid-only cycling and escalate toward pleural biopsy, image-guided biopsy, or pleuroscopy when suspicion remains high.
twoPlus.teachingPoint: Repeated nondiagnostic cytology should not falsely reassure when imaging, history, or recurrence keeps MPE likely.

one.recommendation: A second cytology sample can be considered in selected cases, but tissue strategy should already be visible if pretest probability is high.
one.teachingPoint: One nondiagnostic tap is a fork: repeat selectively, but start planning tissue diagnosis when suspicion stays high.

zero.recommendation: Send adequate cytology and pair the result with imaging, lung expansion, symptoms, and patient goals.
zero.teachingPoint: Thoracentesis can diagnose some MPE, but negative cytology is not a rule-out test.

branch.pleurodesisCandidate: Expandable lung can be considered for talc pleurodesis, IPC, or combined outpatient strategy depending on goals and fitness.
branch.ipcOrRapidPleurodesis: Partial expansion favors IPC-centered care or selected combined/rapid pleurodesis strategy rather than assuming talc alone will work.
branch.ipcPreferred: Trapped or non-expandable lung makes pleurodesis unlikely to succeed; IPC-centered symptom control is the core teaching branch.

yield.thoracentesis: Thoracentesis cytology sensitivity is taught as roughly 40-60%, so negative results require context.
yield.pleuroscopy: Pleuroscopy or pleural biopsy usually offers higher-yield tissue diagnosis, around 80-90% in this teaching context.

management.thoraReasonable: Thoracentesis may be reasonable if the pocket is safe and the clinical question requires sampling or symptom relief.
management.considerTubeAndAdjuncts: Consider tube drainage and adjuncts when infection, blood, loculation, or malignant complexity fits the case.

patternTeaching.simpleAnechoic: Simple anechoic fluid can be a transudate or exudate; the image does not replace clinical context or pleural fluid analysis.
patternTeaching.complexNonSeptated: Complex nonseptated fluid may still be sampled safely when the pocket is accessible, but the broader story decides urgency.
patternTeaching.septatedLoculated: Septations or locules suggest fibrin, infection, blood, or malignant complexity and should prompt drainage/source-control thinking when the clinical context fits.
patternTeaching.echogenic: Echogenic fluid raises concern for pus, blood, cellular debris, or malignancy; do not treat it as a simple free-flowing effusion.
patternTeaching.noDrainableEffusion: This view does not show a drainable pleural fluid pocket. B-lines, A-lines, or subpleural consolidation may answer a lung question, but they are not a thoracentesis target.

patternReveal.simpleAnechoic: The teaching target is a simple anechoic pocket; simple appearance does not prove a transudate.
patternReveal.complexNonSeptated: The teaching target is complex nonseptated fluid with internal echoes but no clear fibrin strands.
patternReveal.septatedLoculated: The teaching target is septated or loculated fluid, suggesting fibrinous organization.
patternReveal.echogenic: The teaching target is echogenic pleural material; pus, blood, cellular debris, or malignancy can create this appearance.
patternReveal.noDrainableEffusion: The teaching target is a lung pattern without a drainable pleural fluid pocket in this view.

dynamicTeaching.normalALines: A-lines are horizontal reverberation artifacts from aerated lung. They are useful distractors in a pleural module because they do not create a drainage target.
dynamicTeaching.bLinesPleuralIrregularity: B-lines arise from the pleural line and move with lung sliding. They answer an interstitial or inflammatory lung question, but they are not a thoracentesis target.
dynamicTeaching.subpleuralConsolidation: Subpleural consolidation can sit right against the pleura and mimic a procedural target at first glance. The key is to keep scanning for an actual fluid window.
dynamicTeaching.lungCurtainNoTarget: The curtain sign is dynamic aerated lung movement. In a pleural procedure module it is a critical no-target pattern, especially near the diaphragm.
dynamicTeaching.effusionAdjacentConsolidation: Fluid plus consolidated lung should shift thinking away from “simple tap” autopilot and toward infection, access-window adequacy, and source-control planning.

dynamicReveal.normalALines: The teaching target is normal A-line reverberation below a sliding pleural line.
dynamicReveal.bLinesPleuralIrregularity: The teaching target is B-line activity with pleural-line irregularity, not a pleural fluid pocket.
dynamicReveal.subpleuralConsolidation: The teaching target is subpleural consolidation with pleural-line irregularity.
dynamicReveal.lungCurtainNoTarget: The teaching target is a lung curtain sweeping over the liver, not a safe fluid pocket.
dynamicReveal.effusionAdjacentConsolidation: The teaching target is effusion with adjacent consolidation, a higher-risk context than an isolated simple pocket.

emerging.metadataDescription: FDA Breakthrough Device designated technologies in interventional pulmonology, recorded for orientation and deliberately excluded from preference-card selection.
emerging.heading: Breakthrough-designated devices
emerging.description: FDA Breakthrough Device designation means the agency agreed to review a device on an expedited path. It is not clearance, it is not approval, and it does not permit US marketing. These entries exist so the catalog can name what is coming without implying any of it is stocked — none of them can be added to a preference card.
emerging.noRoles: No catalog requirement maps to it yet.
emerging.excludedNotice: Excluded from every requirement, picker, and saved card by design.
emerging.evidenceCaveat: Every entry here rests on secondary, AI-generated research rather than a manufacturer document or an FDA decision record. Designation dates come from company announcements in most cases. Re-verify against the FDA PMA, 510(k), and De Novo databases before relying on anything below.
